teaser: Its first recorded viewers called him an astrologer. Its most infamous owner stamped a swastika on it.
review_notes:
Opening: the earliest known record is the Rotterdam sale of 27 April 1713, where the Astronomer and the Geographer were sold as a pair and described as 'An Astrologer' with its companion (wording varies in later sales: 'astrologist', 'mathematical artist'). Used as the 'first audience' because no earlier reaction survives.
Christiaan Huygens: discovery of Saturn's moon Titan (1655) and pendulum clock (1656).
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek born in Delft in 1632 (same year as Vermeer), executor/trustee of Vermeer's bankrupt estate in 1676; identification as the model is speculation, stated as such.
Celestial globe by Jodocus Hondius (1600); book identified as Adriaan Metius, Institutiones Astronomicae et Geographicae, 1621 edition, open at Book III, whose text recommends 'inspiration from God' alongside geometry and instruments (identification by James Welu).
Astrolabe lying on the table: the flat brass disc partly under the carpet, as usually identified; only its edge is clear in our image.
Date MDCLXVIII on the cabinet: only the end (CLXVIII) is legible in our image; some scholars have questioned whether the inscription is original. Only three dated Vermeers (Procuress 1656, Astronomer 1668, Geographer 1669).
'Japanese gown' (Japonse rok) as scholar's dress: standard.
Painting on the wall = Finding of Moses; Moses 'learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians' (Acts 7:22): standard reading.
Seized in 1940 from Edouard de Rothschild in Paris; destined for Hitler's planned museum in Linz; small black swastika stamped on the back; recovered in 1945 (Altaussee salt mine); entered the Louvre in 1983 in lieu of inheritance tax.
Size about 51 x 45 cm. Geographer in the Städel Museum, Frankfurt.

lesson.text: “An Astrologer.” That is how the first people to put this painting into words described it, in a Rotterdam auction list of 1713, where it was sold as a pair with a second scholar picture. Nobody corrected them. Reading the stars to map the sky and reading them to tell fortunes were still close cousins.

Vermeer painted it in 1668, in a country gripped by new science. A Dutchman, Christiaan Huygens, had just found a moon circling Saturn and built the first pendulum clock. Dutch ships crossed oceans by the stars. A man bent over a globe had become a hero worth hanging on the wall, as saints had been a century before.

The pioneer of the microscope, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, was born in Delft in 1632, the same year as Vermeer, and after the painter's death he was put in charge of his bankrupt estate. Some like to think he posed for this picture. No document says so.

Notice what is missing: there is no telescope, and the window shows no sky. This astronomer works indoors, from instruments and books. Vermeer painted those so exactly that historians have managed to trace the real objects he must have had in front of him.

lesson.title: The tools on the table
lesson.text: Three objects, from the brightest to the hardest to see.

spots.title: The globe
spots.text: Not the Earth: a celestial globe, a map of the stars. Constellations appear as beasts and figures. It matches a model sold in Amsterdam in 1600 by the mapmaker Jodocus Hondius.

spots.title: The astrolabe
spots.text: Half hidden where the carpet is pushed back lies a flat brass disc. An astrolabe measured how high a star stood above the horizon.

spots.title: The open book
spots.text: A printed handbook of astronomy, with a pair of dividers lying beside it. The page can be matched to a real edition of 1621.

lesson.text: The book is a manual by Adriaan Metius, a Dutch professor, and it lies open at the start of its third part. That page tells the student what the study of the stars requires: geometry, good instruments and, first of all, inspiration from God. In 1668 science and faith shared a desk.

Vermeer almost never dated his work. Only three of his paintings carry a year, and this is one of them. He did not put it in a corner of the canvas. He wrote it inside the room, as if someone had lettered it onto the furniture.
The year is written in Roman numerals somewhere in this study. Can you find it?

spots.title: On the cabinet door
spots.text: Faint letters on the cupboard, just beyond his fingertips: the end of MDCLXVIII, which is 1668. Above it hangs a chart of circles and lines, another tool of the trade.

lesson.text: The companion picture, “The Geographer,” is dated a year later and now hangs in Frankfurt. Same long-haired young man, same corner by the window, same cabinet. One scholar measures the heavens, the other the Earth. Vermeer painted men alone only in these two canvases.

His loose blue-green robe was a status symbol. Dutch traders in Japan received silk kimonos as gifts, and back home the “Japanese gown” became the favorite indoor dress of scholars and rich merchants. Demand was so high that imitations were sewn locally.
How do you paint thinking? You cannot show an idea. Vermeer shows a body in the half second when an idea arrives, and he uses the direction of the light and of the limbs to do it.
Follow the light first, then the man.

lines.label: From the window
lines.text: Daylight enters at the left and strikes the globe first. The sphere is the brightest object in the room, brighter than his face.

lines.label: His gaze
lines.text: His eyes and the globe sit at almost the same height. The look is level and close, the look of someone checking one precise spot.

lines.label: Rising from the chair
lines.text: His body makes one slanting line from the chair to the fingertips on the globe. He is not sitting back: he has half risen to reach.

lesson.text: The other hand tells the same story. It grips the edge of the table to steady him as he leans. Turning the globe with two fingers, he seems to be checking the stars against what he has just read in the book. It is a small movement, and the picture holds its breath around it.

On the right wall, lost in shadow, hangs a painting of the baby Moses found in his basket on the Nile. An odd choice for a study, until you learn that the Bible calls Moses learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. To people of the time he was the oldest scientist of all.
Vermeer gave a scholar the stillness and the light he usually gave to women pouring milk or reading letters. Looking hard at something becomes the action.

The painting's later life was less peaceful. In the 1880s it entered the Paris collection of the Rothschild banking family. In 1940, after the German army took the city, Nazi agents seized it from Édouard de Rothschild. Adolf Hitler wanted it for the giant museum he planned in Linz, the Austrian town of his youth.
The looters marked their prize. A small swastika was stamped in black ink on the back of the canvas, where it remains part of the object's history.

Allied soldiers recovered it in 1945 and it went back to the family. In 1983 the Rothschilds handed it to France in place of inheritance taxes, and it entered the Louvre. The pair sold together in Rotterdam now lives in two countries. Only an exhibition, now and then, puts the two scholars side by side again.

quiz.question: How was the painting described at its first recorded sale in 1713?
quiz.explanation: The auction list called it “An Astrologer.”

quiz.question: What kind of globe is he touching?
options: A celestial globe, showing the stars
quiz.explanation: It is a celestial globe with the constellations drawn as figures.

quiz.question: Where did Vermeer write the year 1668?
options: On the cabinet, in Roman numerals
quiz.explanation: The date MDCLXVIII is lettered on the cupboard door.

quiz.question: Why is a painting of Moses on the wall?
options: Moses was seen as a man of ancient learning
quiz.explanation: The Bible calls Moses learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

quiz.question: What was the scholar's robe modeled on?
quiz.explanation: The “Japanese gown” copied silk kimonos given to Dutch traders in Japan.

quiz.question: How did the painting enter the Louvre in 1983?
options: It was given in place of inheritance taxes
It was found in an attic
quiz.explanation: The Rothschild family handed it to the French state instead of paying inheritance taxes.

facts.text: The astronomer is looking at the night sky through a telescope.
facts.explanation: There is no telescope: he works indoors with a globe, an astrolabe and a book.

facts.text: The Nazis stamped a swastika on the back of the canvas.
facts.explanation: After seizing it in 1940 they marked it with a small black swastika.

facts.text: We know for certain that the model was the microscope pioneer Leeuwenhoek.
facts.explanation: It is a popular guess, but no document supports it.
